Hi,

Thanks for the super quick response. You are correct that my example (and real world use case that this example is based on) is strictly within the context of a console app that makes HTTP requests as part of an ETL process, so ASP.NET Core is not even in the picture.

Looking at your code sample, it looks like the shorter call timeout is being handled by the creation of a `CancellationToken` based on a 1-second timespan instead of the explicit Timeout policy.  Is my understanding correct?

So in that example, you'd have a 60 second timeout on the `HttpClient`, then a 10 second pessimistic timeout policy with Polly, and then a 1 second timeout from the call site via the `CancellationToken`.

In practice that'd mean your individual requests would time out after 1 second and then do a decorrelated jitter retry until it either exhausted the retries or hit the overall 10 second timeout configured on the timeout policy.

> So in that example, you'd have a 60 second timeout on the `HttpClient`, then a 10 second pessimistic timeout policy with Polly, and then a 1 second timeout from the call site via the `CancellationToken`.

Wait a minute, so you're saying that my original code example with the Timeout policy would _indeed_ be switching to pessimistic due to its inability to pass around the `CancellationToken`? That's [surprising to me](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Polly-and-HttpClientFactory#use-case-applying-timeouts) because the documentation here says that it's supposed to be optimistic by default.

At any rate, I do think that the [documentation for Polly and HttpClientFactory](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Polly-and-HttpClientFactory) needs to be updated to reflect this particular scenario. The [Timeout documentation](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Timeout) gives plenty of examples where `ExecuteAsync` is used, but none for when the (admittedly confusing) DI framework with `HttpClientFactory` is being used.

Edit: The big implication here is that for per-call timeouts, you're better off just using `CancellationTokenSource.Token` like you suggested instead of a specific Timeout policy when dealing with `HttpClientFactory` and the `HttpClient` objects it spits out.

Sorry, you're right, what I wrote was incorrect. The overall timeout would be 1 second if you passed through the `CancellationToken` because the inner policies would "give up" when the cancellation was triggered.

A policy cannot "switch" between pessimistic and optimistic. It's always whatever you specified when you created it, which in your example is optimistic.

For your use case, I'd review what exactly the behaviour you'd expect to be is. The choice of pessimistic vs optimistic is going to be a function of how you want it to retry, if you have client-specified timeouts, or you don't and that's what you want the timeout policy to achieve. It will depend on the relative values of those.

Regarding documentation, we have #853 to update any out-of-date documentation, but the `HttpClientFactory` integration is a bit of a grey area as the implementation is actually in the [ASP.NET Core repo](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/6ac8ebc38cd43027efb4b2cbb32599befe9a6f60/src/HttpClientFactory/Polly/src/PolicyHttpMessageHandler.cs#L131), and there's further documentation of their own [here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/implement-resilient-applications/use-httpclientfactory-to-implement-resilient-http-requests) and [here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/implement-resilient-applications/implement-http-call-retries-exponential-backoff-polly).

> Regarding documentation, we have #853 to update any out-of-date documentation, but the `HttpClientFactory` integration is a bit of a grey area as the implementation is actually in the [ASP.NET Core repo](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/6ac8ebc38cd43027efb4b2cbb32599befe9a6f60/src/HttpClientFactory/Polly/src/PolicyHttpMessageHandler.cs#L131), and there's further documentation of their own [here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/implement-resilient-applications/use-httpclientfactory-to-implement-resilient-http-requests) and [here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/implement-resilient-applications/implement-http-call-retries-exponential-backoff-polly).

Oof, so that explains why a lot of the documentation regarding `HttpClientFactory` keeps squawking about crap I don't care about such as `PageModel`. My use case is simply just a console app that gets scheduled to run at specific times via Task Manager in Windows Server and needs to communicate to API endpoints via HTTP. I also like the idea of having a **well-behaved** client app that talks to API endpoints, which is how I stumbled upon Polly and `HttpClientFactory`, which solves the exhausted socket and stale DNS issues.

Anyway, I didn't realize until you told me that `CancellationTokenSource.Token` exists. I might just use that for per-call timeouts instead while leaving the other policies in place. I have another use case where the overall timeout in HttpClient is set to 5 minutes and the per-call timeout has to be 1 minute, so I'm guessing that will change the calculus a bit when deciding between pessimistic vs. optimistic.

Thanks for the discussion. As I continue to work through this console app, I'll make note on which parts of the documentation aren't clear and give feedback (if any) to #853.

> I'll make note on which parts of the documentation aren't clear and give feedback (if any) to https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/issues/853.

Great, thanks!

Note how the documentation says "_**at most** 10 seconds_", not "_**in** 10 seconds_".

A more detailed discussion is given at the bottom of the wiki page you have referenced [here](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Advanced-Circuit-Breaker#detailed-operation-of-failure-statistics).

> Internally, the circuit-breaker measures statistics with a rolling statistical window. The configured samplingDuration T is divided into ten slices, such that statistics for 10% of the period T are discarded every time T / 10. This smooths the calculation of failure rates to acceptable tolerances (compared to disposing 100% of the statistics every time T).
>
> The samplingDuration is not however further subdivided into slices if samplingDuration is set below 200 milliseconds. This prevents excessively frequent recalculation when there is little responsiveness gain.

Depending on how the advanced circuit breaker is configured, it either uses a fixed window of time, or a rolling window of time. The time is calculated in either case based on the progression of the wall clock time from the system clock via `DateTime.UtcNow`.

comments.body: I should note that I am using the latest release of Polly v7.2.2

There's two issues with your code here that explain the behaviour you're observing vs. what you expect.

1. A circuit breaker policy does not retry. For retries, you would use a [retry policy](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly#retry). A [circuit breaker](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly#circuit-breaker) policy will throw any exception observed out to the caller _unless_ the circuit breaks - at which point it throws `BrokenCircuitException`. This is why your code fails at the first step, because the code it is executing throws an exception. With enough failures, the circuit breaker would bypass the delegate you pass to `Execute()`, and just throw `BrokenCircuitException`.
2. Your policy only handles `TimeoutException`, so even if it behaved as you expected, it wouldn't retry or circuit break for any of the other cases because they do not throw `TimeoutException` (or an exception derived from it), so would throw the exception to the calling method and not trigger any circuit breaking behaviour.

From your sample, it seems like you want to use a [policy wrap](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly#policywrap) composed of a retry policy wrapped with a circuit breaker that stops all calls if too many calls fail.
@martincostello I thought I would follow up. Is there another policy I can wrap this with to avoid doing the try/catch and timeout's myself? Thanks for your help!
You would typically use a [PolicyWrap](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly#policywrap) to combine different policies together.
I guess there's no option and circuit breaker just wasn't meant for this scenario. Thanks anyway.

comments.body:
You're doing `.Result` on a Task from the ASP.NET controller.

This is a well-known way to create a deadlock when running under IIS in .NET Framework due to the way the threading model/synchronisation context works.

Change the controller method to be async and await the call, I'm pretty sure it will resolve the deadlock.

https://blog.stephencleary.com/2012/07/dont-block-on-async-code.html

Solved! 

In TestController.cs I just changed the following line:
```csharp
var response = PollyTestRequest.Send().Result;
```

To: 
```csharp
var response = Task.Run(async () => await PollyTestRequest.Send()).Result;
```

Thanks for your help!

The problem here is that you're trying to do async as part of the `OrResult` which from looking at the code doesn't _seem_ to be supported as it's not inherently async so wouldn't be awaited internally. Also `HandleTransientHttpError()` is built around `HttpResponseMessage` and not `Task<HttpResponseMessage>`.

https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly.Extensions.Http/blob/69fd292bc603cb3032e57b028522737255f03a49/src/Polly.Extensions.Http/HttpPolicyExtensions.cs#L43

You could build a policy yourself to change the result type to handle it yourself fairly easily from the building blocks, but I still think there'd be a problem with the async call to ReadAsStringAsync() as part of the `OrResult()`.

From the looks of things, the matching predicates are all based around `bool` not `Task<bool>`, so you'd only be able to get it working with something like `GetAwaiter().GetResult()` or `.Result` in the `OrResult()` lambda, but I wouldn't recommend that as you'd probably end up deadlocking something:

If you'd like to have a try and implementing it and seeing what changes would be involved, I'd be happy to review any resulting PR. comments.body:
.NET guidance is that _libraries_ always specify `ConfigureAwait(false)`, so as far as I'm aware that's what we do as Polly is a library. There's a great blog post by Stephen Toub on the .NET team [here](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/configureawait-faq/).

The specific call-out for this is quoted below from [this section](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/configureawait-faq/#when-should-i-use-configureawaitfalse):

> if you’re writing general-purpose library code, use ConfigureAwait(false)

It's not scalable for every async API everywhere (not just in Polly, but throughout the .NET runtime) to have parameters to do this. If you need to use `true`, you should specify that in the appropriate points in your own code when you call async methods.

> It's not scalable for every async API everywhere (not just in Polly, but throughout the .NET runtime) to have parameters to do this. If you need to use `true`, you should specify that in the appropriate points in your own code when you call async methods.

I would agree with you, but since you already have extension points in ExecuteAndCaptureAsync and ExecuteAsync overloads with continueOnCapturedContext flag I don't see why it would be hard to extend this further? This seems very inconsistent API, and consistency I think is what makes a good library. 
As of your comment, we are specifying true where we need, but we cannot use Polly everywhere we want because of this issue. If we do we are basically losing the MVC HttpContext and sometimes we get errors that depend on the context with subsequent code. We already registered one bug and solved it in regards to that:
https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/issues/674

Let me know if you need further details or explanation on the issue. Thanks for quick reply.

Simonas

We can see what other people think in the team and community, I'm just giving my own opinion, but adding lots of extra options in all the different overloads for all the different policies that have async will lead to even more combinations of code paths and configuration to deal with that isn't strictly necessary, increasing the amount of things to maintain and test.

The number of parameters on policies is already causing pain and is being considered to be revisited for Polly v8, so maybe something like this would be more workable in a rethink of how configuration works, but at the moment I think it would probably cause a lot of extra maintenance burden and complexity relative to the gain.

In the issue you reference, that's a bug in functionality that existed already. This seems to be about extending it further, which is where the maintainability argument comes in on whether that's the _right_ thing to do.

> The number of parameters on policies is already causing pain and is being considered to be revisited for Polly v8, so maybe something like this would be more workable in a rethink of how configuration works, but at the moment I think it would probably cause a lot of extra maintenance burden and complexity relative to the gain.

I agree that having that amount of parameters to Execute methods seems like an overkill. Maybe it's worth allowing to build configuration in following manner:
return Policy
                **.ContinueOnCapturedContext(true)**
                .HandleResult<HttpResponseMessage>(response => !response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
                .Or<Exception>()
                .WaitAndRetryAsync(_maxRetryAttempts, SleepDurationProvider);

That would allow avoiding arguments to Execute, but not sure how much refactoring it would take to actually do it.

I am hearing your opinion though. We'll switch from Polly for now with own retry mechanism to workaround it for now.

Simonas

Have you considered using a _real_ circuit breaker policy in your tests, rather than the interfaces, and then testing your code that way?

Mocking the policies won't test whether you've configured your policies correctly to get the behaviour you actually want at runtime, for example.

I've had this problem in the past where my assumptions about how Polly works were incorrect and then the mocks just reflected those incorrect assumptions, leading to bugs even though the tests passed.

@martincostello I don't want to unit test policy itself. I would like to test my business code properly that's relay on policy.

When I can't mock ie `breaker.CircuitState` then I can't write properly unit test that checks is something going to happen when circuit breaker is open.

I'm not suggesting you unit test the policy, I'm suggesting your test your code that _uses_ policies. You can do that without needing mocks for circuit breakers.

If you can mock the _action_ wrapped in the policy to throw an appropriate exception for your usage, then the circuit breaker will trip (assuming you've configured it correctly) and test your business logic handles it appropriately.

Otherwise you're coupling your tests too much to the implementation details of Polly. There's not much need to mock out Polly because it's not doing any I/O or other things where mocks are more useful (like calling an API or reading from a database).

I'm just suggesting you adapt your test approach to test your code in a different way, removing the need for you to "solve" this mocking problem.

If for some philosophical reason you don't want to do that, then that's fine and that's your choice. But it's not how I'd go about testing business logic that relied on Polly myself for reasons including the ones I mentioned above, which is why this is my suggestion.

comments.body:
I step-debugged into the source code for [Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection/) and found what I believe to be the cause of the deadlock triggered by your original code.

Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection [takes out a lock](https://github.com/dotnet/extensions/blob/32cc8162ff38356b293611138d361f757a62e025/src/DependencyInjection/DI/src/ServiceLookup/CallSiteRuntimeResolver.cs#L82) when the DI resolves a singleton (or scoped service for any given scope).  The DI code checks whether the singleton (or instance for that scope) has already been generated and cached, and if not, invokes the constructor and caches the result. The lock is used to ensure only one instance (per scope) is created.

This sequence appears to cause the deadlock (when both `MainApp` and `IEIAuthentication` are configured as singleton via `services.AddSingleton<T>()`):

1. The DI takes out a lock to ensure a singleton of `MainApp`, and invokes the `MainApp` constructor.
2. The `MainApp` constructor successfully retrieves the `EiHttpClient`-named-client configuration from HttpClientFactory.
3. The `MainApp` constructor then executes through `httpClient.GetAsync(new Uri(url))` with a call which invokes the configured Policy, and the policy tries to resolve the second singleton: `services2.GetService<IEIAuthentication>()`.  (And the execution has moved to a different thread: I forgot to note during step-debugging whether this happened at the point of an async Task invocation during the httpClient call, or if the DI resolver [forked the singleton resolution to a new thread](https://github.com/dotnet/extensions/blob/32cc8162ff38356b293611138d361f757a62e025/src/DependencyInjection/DI/src/ServiceLookup/CallSiteRuntimeResolver.cs#L76-L79); but the debug view in Visual Studio confirms the two threads.)
4. Trying to resolve the second singleton tries to take out the lock-for-resolving-singletons, but that lock is held by another thread because we are blocked on the result of the Http call during executing the constructor of `MainApp` - deadlock!

---

I tested, and using the Async Initialization pattern (see previous comment) solves this. In that variant, the constructor of `MainApp` stores the `Task` returned for the async call, and this is returned before the async call reaches trying to resolve the second singleton; hence no deadlock.

As the deadlock only occurs when the DI has to create the instances of both singletons for you, you can also remove the deadlock by creating at least one of the two singletons yourself at DI registration-time, eg:

    services.AddSingleton<MainApp>();
    services.AddSingleton<IEIAuthentication>(new EIAuthenticationService());

However, not blocking on async work in the constructor of `MainApp` would be preferable.

Closing, as a diagnosis and several resolutions have been provided, and there is nothing we can change in the Polly codebase around this.  If you have further questions though, just post and we can re-open.

You could also raise this with the [dotnet/extensions](https://github.com/dotnet/extensions/) team, who own both the HttpClientFactory and DI code, but I wouldn't be surprised if the response was that heavy-lifting (such as making and blocking on async calls) during a constructor is not recommended or supported.

title: Change all policy configuration to return policies as interfaces

comments.body:
Thanks @jjxtra for the suggestion! Declarative attributing to apply policies is an interesting idea, and came up once before.

The biggest potential drawback I can see - if the attributes configure the policies themselves - is that attributes require parameters to be compile-time constants (eg `[Retry(3)]`).  This tends either to preclude or not play well with various other policy features - driving policies from external config; using any policy-callback features like `onRetry`; using anything dynamic at runtime like enumerables for delay-between-retries, eg for [jitter](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Retry-with-jitter); and DI/separation-of-concerns and unit-testing. 

We have tended to adopt/recommend injecting policies or a [PolicyRegistry](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/PolicyRegistry) into consuming code by DI, to decouple the operation governed from the policy applied to it; which in turn facilities various dimensions of [unit-testing](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Unit-testing-with-Polly---with-examples). Using PolicyRegistry can also enable [dynamic reconfiguration during running, driven by config changes](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Dynamic-reconfiguration-during-running).

Are there ways an attribute-declarative approach could bridge those issues?  One idea could be an attribute which simply applies a policy from a PolicyRegistry:

    [ApplyPolicy(string policyKey)]
    Task<string> FetchJson1Async(string param1);

This could have the benefit that there is only one attribute to build 🙂 , and give flexibility to vary policies at runtime and in unit tests. The attribute would need to be able to statically access a common PolicyRegistry - could lead to that PolicyRegistry being a process-wide singleton (ambient-context pattern) or similar?

Thoughts welcome!

We'd love to see more on this if this is something you (or anyone) want/s to develop and contribute as a [Polly-Contrib](https://github.com/Polly-Contrib/) project. (For clarity, I am not expecting to spend any of my own time on this, compared to other Polly priorities I have.)

---

You might also be interested to dig around the [PollyNator project](https://github.com/Pro-Coded/Polly.Contrib.Pollynator). This takes a Roslyn-code-generation approach to generating a Polly decorator for an interface.

PollyNator does wrap an interface using Roslyn so that's interesting. It does not use attributes but rather a class-wide policy. With a little work it could probably be tweaked to do attributes instead. That would cover the second suggestion.

For the first suggestion, your idea of using a policy key seems like it would work well, allowing the policy to be configured and injected at runtime.

Thanks for your well thought out response, Polly is an amazing library, I have only stumbled upon it recently and have been using it for https://ipban.com back-end :)
This idea is great！Is there a plan?

> The biggest potential drawback I can see - if the attributes configure the policies themselves - is that attributes require parameters to be compile-time constants (eg [Retry(3)]). This tends either to preclude or not play well with various other policy features - driving policies from external config; using any policy-callback features like onRetry; using anything dynamic at runtime like enumerables for delay-between-retries, eg for jitter; and DI/separation-of-concerns and unit-testing.

We could use the best of both worlds. My preferred item for comparison is [Java's Spring Retry](https://docs.spring.io/spring-retry/docs/api/current/org/springframework/retry/annotation/Retryable.html) annotation, where you **can't** set a configurable policy but are restrained to compile-time retry policy.

So the new Polly-Contrib project could allow both a compile-time and registry policy giving priority to any if both are chosen (or error).

As for the very implementation in DI framework, as a very experienced Spring contributor, I'd investigate how can .NET Core DI handle AOP (Aspect Oriented Programming) via interception, something like `PollyNator does wrap an interface` statement.

We should make plans, I'm interested in this topic for my company.

See also

- https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/26942
- https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/36021

[Fody](https://github.com/Fody/Fody) could satisfy the AOP requirement above.

Some [features](https://github.com/castleproject/Core/issues/145) requested to [Castle.Core.AsyncInterceptor](https://github.com/JSkimming/Castle.Core.AsyncInterceptor) (which is runtime generated rather than compile time like Fody) allow for re-entrancy, which would be required to wrap with Polly, so it should be doable there (there's an issue [discussing that scenario](https://github.com/JSkimming/Castle.Core.AsyncInterceptor/issues/52))

With Fody, ideally we'd not be manipulating IL directly since there are [many](https://github.com/csnemes/tracer/issues/88) difficult [problems](https://github.com/csnemes/tracer/issues/81) but there are some libraries that may help...
- https://github.com/vescon/MethodBoundaryAspect.Fody
- https://github.com/csnemes/tracer

I'm not sure either of these will support re-writing the return value, though, which we would need to do to say 'don't return _that_ Task, return _our_ Task'. Castle.Core.AsyncInterceptor does support this, but at the cost of not being as performant as compile-time generated code.
backref to `duplicate`: https://github.com/vescon/MethodBoundaryAspect.Fody/issues/91
@martincostello think we should close this. IMO AOP is not really something Polly should dable in

I would agree that this isn't something that should really live in the core - it would add a lot of additional complexity and support burden (IMHO).

Seems like a candidate for something that builds on top of Polly in the [Polly-Contrib](https://github.com/Polly-Contrib) to me.

comments.body:
A couple of technical comments about the [original quoted code](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/issues/732#issue-540316759), in case you eventually settle on a solution more like that.

First, with `.WaitAndRetryAsync(...)`, you don't need to manually call `await Task.Delay(type1Intervals.ElementAt(retryCount))` yourself.  The call to `await Task.Delay(...)` is [already built in to the policy implementation](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/4db50346299f62c2373ceba99d2522a8171c9e27/src/Polly/Retry/AsyncRetryEngine.cs#L80).  You only need to configure the policy to specify the delay timespans, as shown in [the readme examples for WaitAndRetry](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly#wait-and-retry).  

Second, be aware that:

    var type1Intervals = GetRetryIntervals(10, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100), TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(10000));

with

    type1Intervals.ElementAt(retryCount)

will [get a new enumerator at each call to `.ElementAt(...)`](https://github.com/microsoft/referencesource/blob/3b1eaf5203992df69de44c783a3eda37d3d4cd10/System.Core/System/Linq/Enumerable.cs#L1236), and thus each call to `.ElementAt(retryCount)` in your original code will in fact be based on a different, freshly-realised sequence of the enumerable.  With the original code, you might want to add a `.ToList()` or `.ToArray()` thus: 

    var type1Intervals = GetRetryIntervals(...).ToArray();

to reify the sequence just once.

@FrancescoReviso The code in the [comment above](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/issues/732#issuecomment-567861282) will apply the "type 1" WaitAndRetry behaviour to any `exception is Type1Exception`, and the other WaitAndRetry behaviour to all other exceptions.

Re:

>Is it also possible to apply an "except logic" to the exception thrown? 
>Suppose I would like to apply a WaitAndRetry behaviour for all the types of exceptions except one, in this case Type1Exception

If you want the WaitAndRetry policy to _not apply at all_ for one exception type, you can make a policy to handle all exceptions except that, by using a single handle clause like this:

    .Handle<Exception>(e => !(e is Type1Exception))

comments.body:
See the documentation on [TimeoutPolicy with `TimeoutStrategy.Pessimistic`](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Timeout#pessimistic-timeout). In this mode, the timed-out action is not cancelled: it is [passed as the `task` property to the `onTimeoutAsync` delegate, and you can attach a continuation to capture what eventually happens](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Timeout#pessimistic-timeout-1).

The parallel calls will of course consume more resource - the new calls (retries) will run in parallel with the continuing old (walked-away-from) calls. If that's an issue, a compromise could be to have this mode as an option, which you can switch on in production to gather more diagnostic information, when relevant.

@aalia You're right. In principle, `TimeoutStrategy.Pessimistic` _can_ achieve what you asked (not cancel and capture the outcome of the walked-away-from task), but there is an additional requirement: the delegate executed through the policy must also ignore any `CancellationToken` passed to it. 

_Explanation_: In `TimeoutStrategy.Pessimistic` [the implementation does still pass the policy's timing-out CancellationToken to the executed code](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/793eb8edac13fbdefc78978ed738481bdea1270d/src/Polly/Timeout/AsyncTimeoutEngine.cs#L41-L43).  This was an intentional design choice, for two reasons: (i) it is still always preferable, resource-wise, to cancel if possible; (ii) it allows `TimeoutStrategy.Pessimistic` to be used on underlying code which mixes elements which do and don't honour cancellation.

So the behaviour you are seeking is not possible with off-the-shelf timeout policy configured via the existing HttpClientFactory methods.

---

To achieve what you asked, you would have to create code to not pass the `CancellationToken` into lower levels of the http call.  You could do any one of:

(1) Code a simple [`DelegatingHandler`](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.http.delegatinghandler) overriding [`SendAsync()`](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.http.delegatinghandler.sendasync) to not pass on the supplied `CancellationToken`, and insert that into the HttpClient configuration on HttpClientFactory, inside the TimeoutPolicy (list it after the TimeoutPolicy), using the [`.AddHttpMessageHandler<THandler>()` overload](https://github.com/aspnet/Extensions/blob/f12d709976e382672ce100bc00381a8847f06489/src/HttpClientFactory/Http/src/DependencyInjection/HttpClientBuilderExtensions.cs#L154-L155) 

_or_

(2) Code your own custom handler similar to [`PolicyHttpMessageHandler`](https://github.com/aspnet/Extensions/blob/f12d709976e382672ce100bc00381a8847f06489/src/HttpClientFactory/Polly/src/PolicyHttpMessageHandler.cs), but make the [underlying http execution](https://github.com/aspnet/Extensions/blob/f12d709976e382672ce100bc00381a8847f06489/src/HttpClientFactory/Polly/src/PolicyHttpMessageHandler.cs#L130) intentionally ignore the passed CancellationToken - something like this:

      response = await policy.ExecuteAsync((c, ct) => SendCoreAsync(request, c, CancellationToken.None), context, cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);

_or_

(3) Code your own timeout policy as a [custom proactive Policy](http://www.thepollyproject.org/2019/02/13/authoring-a-proactive-polly-policy-custom-policies-part-ii/) which does not [pass the policy's timing-out CancellationToken to the executed code](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/793eb8edac13fbdefc78978ed738481bdea1270d/src/Polly/Timeout/AsyncTimeoutEngine.cs#L41-L43)

---

Note that any of (1) (2) or (3) will also lose you other uses of cancellation through `HttpClient`, such as:

+ [cancelling all pending requests via `CancelPendingRequests()` and `Dispose()`](https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/blob/c63fbb73226ae3de3ee38d9b25de24ed3e41b6e2/src/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/HttpClient.cs#L613-L648)
+ the overall timeout provided by `HttpClient.Timeout`, which [also operates by `CancellationToken`](https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/blob/c63fbb73226ae3de3ee38d9b25de24ed3e41b6e2/src/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/HttpClient.cs#L481-L489)

---

_To re-iterate downsides/cautions about doing this in production_:  Given this approach effectively chooses to suspend any local timeout, you risk the app tieing up resources waiting for responses which never come - this could become a resource issue which affects your application performance over time. If the called system is under your control, it may be more effective to instrument the called system to determine why it isn't responding in a timely fashion.
Closing due to no further questions at this time.  If you have further questions, please post again (or start a new issue), and we will gladly pick up the conversation.

Hi @reisenberger -- just following up on this. This statement:
> In TimeoutStrategy.Pessimistic [the implementation does still pass the policy's timing-out CancellationToken to the executed code](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/793eb8edac13fbdefc78978ed738481bdea1270d/src/Polly/Timeout/AsyncTimeoutEngine.cs#L41-L43). This was an intentional design choice, for two reasons: (i) it is still always preferable, resource-wise, to cancel if possible; (ii) it allows TimeoutStrategy.Pessimistic to be used on underlying code which mixes elements which do and don't honour cancellation.

Is true in theory... but doesn't seem to be in practice, we've observed the downstream cancellation token not being cancelled. This isn't apparent in unit tests, because the UT SystemClock actually cancels the downstream token as part of it's behaviour in a timeout.

I have a branch with a test, and fix for this will post the PR.

Hi and thanks for replying.

I wasn't aware of the "single trial per break duration rule" when the circuit is in the **half-open** state. I actually read about it in the documentation, but I didn't fully understand all the implications of that. 

So, just to summarize, we can state the following:

- when the circuit is in the **half-open** state only one attempt to execute the delegate is permitted during a time frame equals to the configured break duration.
- if this attempt succeeds without throwing any exception, then the circuit moves to the **closed** state. 
- if an exception is thrown during the attempt, **the exception is rethrown by the policy whether or not it is handled by the policy itself**. If the exception is one of the handled exceptions, then the circuit moves to the **open** state. Otherwise, it remains in the **half-open** state. 
 - any other attempt to execute the delegate will be immediately rejected by throwing the `BrokenCircuitException`, without executing the delegate (fail fast approach, the same observed when the circuit is in the **open** state). 
 - if the circuit moves to the **open** state, it will remain open for the entire break duration (as usual). If it remains in the **half-open** state, **other attempts to execute the delegate will be allowed only after a delay equals to the break duration**. Only one attempt is allowed per break duration.

Is all of this correct ?

Thanks!
@EnricoMassoneDeltatre Yes, that's correct.

I support this, in the fact that I also had to hunt around for the `WaitAndRetry` policy info, however.. with a bit of trial and error you can get there in the end 👍🏼.

The first thing to note is that the `sleepDurationProvider` is a `Func()`, and therefore the first two items are inputs, the third being an output.. this is not written in the documentation, as it is a C# concept.

In addition, there are some topics elsewhere on the Wiki, and although they are not _perhaps_ 100% complete.. they go in to some detail:

Hi @cmadhani . If you haven't seen it already, check out as well our specific doco on the [different effects of combining retry with timeout in different orders, in `PolicyWrap`](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Timeout#combining-timeout-with-retries).

With the order you have:

     AsyncPolicyWrap<HttpResponseMessage> policyWrap = timeOutPolicy.WrapAsync(retryPolicy);

the timeout will act as a timeout across _all tries combined_.  IE Once the timeout occurs, no further tries will be permitted - they will be pre-emptively cancelled by the timeout's `CancellationToken` which has signalled (fired).

If you want to use TimeoutPolicy as a timeout-per-try, reverse the order of the policies:

     AsyncPolicyWrap<HttpResponseMessage> policyWrap = retryPolicy.WrapAsync(timeOutPolicy);

Again, more on that in the [doco already linked](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Timeout#combining-timeout-with-retries), and [here](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/PolicyWrap#ordering-the-available-policy-types-in-a-wrap).

comments.body:
@bramakrishna16 . See the comparable reports here: https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/issues/26054 . 

I'm not clear which version of .NET Core / Framework you are using, but it seems that the internal storage for [`HttpHeaders`](https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/blob/master/src/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/Headers/HttpHeaders.cs) is not a thread-safe dictionary - perhaps because concurrent access is not expected.  

From your problem description, it seems possible that the code is causing race conditions (against itself), causing multiple threads to collide in adding to/removing from a non-thread-safe dictionary - hence the exception you are seeing.

Polly in itself is not CPU intensive; is it possible that your retry construction is generating a lot of retries in a tight loop (including retries which overlap), thus high CPU?  (a possibility - without seeing more code/a repro, hard to tell at this stage)

Could you post more complete code? - all policies configured against the given `HttpClient` configuration on `HttpClientFactory`?  (Best of all, a [minimal reproducible example](https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example) demonstrating the problem, if you can make one.)

A common cause for an async retry loop "treading on itself" (getting into a state of multiple tries running concurrently) would be that there is some async call somewhere which is not `await`ed. It would be worth checking that has not crept into the code anywhere.

Thanks @bramakrishna16 . This is what I think is happening.  When you cache the policy in the `IPolicyRegistry<string>`, if the policy is not already there:

    registry[NonRootRetryPolicyName] = policy;

you are caching a `policy` instance with an `onRetryAsync` closure, which closes over (which captures into the closure) the `httpRequestMessage` variable.  That is, the `policy` instance cached in the registry contains a delegate which _captures the single instance of_ `httpRequestMessage` _passed to this method the very first time the method executes, when it caches_ `policy`.

All later executions through the method will not be using the HttpRequestMessage of the later http requests - they will all be using the one single instance `httpRequestMessage` that was passed to the method the first time it executed, which was captured in the closure with the policy.  If this theory is correct, when you have _any_ concurrency of http requests through this policy at a later time, they will be concurrently manipulating the `httpRequestMessage.Headers` dictionary on the same original `httpRequestMessage` instance - hence the exceptions you are seeing arising from concurrently manipulating a non-thread-safe dictionary.

To verify if this theory is correct, just remove all the logic about storing the policy in the policy registry - and see if the problem goes away. (_EDIT:_ I'm referring here to the exception from within `System.Net.Http.Headers.HttpHeaders.ParseRawHeaderValues(...)`).

@bramakrishna16 I have some theories why 100% CPU may be being consumed but not enough information to make a strong guess.  It would probably help if you could post:

+ the code of all policies configured on this HttpClient via `HttpClientFactory`
+ the statement where they are configured on `HttpClientFactory` - ie the code with the `AddPolicyHandler()` calls.  It's important to see the order in which the policies are configured.

And some questions: 

+ What is the `HttpClient.Timeout` property set to?
+ What is the typical value of `settings.NonRootLevelRetryCount`?

Thank you.

Thanks @bramakrishna16 . So the code configuring the policies on HttpClientFactory is something like this: ?

    services.AddHttpClient(/* more configuration */)
        .AddPolicyHandler(SelectTimeoutPolicy)
        .AddPolicyHandler(SelectNonRootLevelRetryPolicy)
        .AddPolicyHandler(SelectRetryTimeoutPolicy);

(Please let me know if that is _not_ the order in which the policy configuration statements appear. Thank you.)
yes, that sounds right! Thank you!

Hi @bramakrishna16 . I cannot see any obvious reasons for high CPU from the policies quoted and the policy sequence.   Polly itself is lightweight and unlikely to be the direct cause of high CPU.

Potential problems I was looking for (in case you find them, maybe in code I have not seen): something like a high `retryCount:` combined with calls which failed immediately and were then retried immediately (the combination could generate a tight loop, exacerbated by high concurrency).  

But the cause of the high CPU could be something entirely different.

It's hard to offer further suggestions without being able to sit next to you and analyse concurrent thread usage  - and what those threads are doing - when the issue occurs. Suggest taking that approach.

---

One caution: `HttpClient.Timeout == TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10)` is likely too low.  When using Polly retries via HttpClientFactory, `HttpClient.Timeout` becomes an overall timeout to each entire call through HttpClient, including all tries and waits between retries (not a timeout-per-try).  See our [documentation on timeouts with HttpClientFactory](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Polly-and-HttpClientFactory#use-case-applying-timeouts). 

With `HttpClient.Timeout` at 10 seconds, that could mean that your retries are failing immediately anyway (if the first try has taken up the 10 seconds). Once the `CancellationToken` associated with `HttpClient.Timeout` has signalled, it is not reset again (cancellation tokens are single-use only) - so the retry may already be marked timed out before it even starts, in which case it would throw immediately.

Since you already have `SelectTimeoutPolicy` as an overall timeout, you could set `HttpClient.Timeout` very high (so as not to interfere). You could also consider using `HttpClient.Timeout` instead of `SelectTimeoutPolicy`, but `HttpClient.Timeout` gives you less clear control. A timeout due to `HttpClient.Timeout` usually manifests as `OperationCanceledException`, which is hard to distinguish from other cancellation.

---

Did removing the policy caching within `SelectNonRootLevelRetryPolicy` help?

@reisenberger, I was able to resolve multiple headers issue after removing the policy caching! I tested it and works. Thank you very much!

I have couple of follow-up questions:

We don't want to create a policy every time because of latency issues. We want to create it once and re-use the same policy.

Can we store it globally and re-use the same policy using this extension - ` AddPolicyHandler()` ? 
Or Can we create our own custom handler for this purpose?

Thanks for your time!

I noticed: you will likely want to make similar changes for the [`SelectTimeoutPolicy` method](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/issues/689#issuecomment-535259620).  This original code in that method:

```csharp
                        var timeoutException = new TimeoutException(string.Format(
                            System.Globalization.CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
                            "Timeout occurred while calling service {0}. Activity ID: {1} StartTimeUTC: {2} EndTimeUTC: {3}, Configured RequestTimeout: {4}ms Task was canceled",
                            httpRequestMessage.RequestUri.ToString(),
                            cxt != null ? cxt.ActivityId : Guid.Empty,
                            now.Subtract(timespan).ToString("HH:mm:ss.fffff", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture),
                            now.ToString("HH:mm:ss.fffff", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture),
                            operationTimeout));
```

has the same closure problem [discussed here](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/issues/689#issuecomment-535226843) - the policy stored in the registry will have an `onTimeoutAsync` delegate which closes over the `httpRequestMessage` instance in scope at the time the policy is stored in the registry. So the logging would always log the `httpRequestMessage.RequestUri` of that first request.

To make sure the policy will log the `httpRequestMessage.RequestUri` of each specific request, you would need to adapt `SelectTimeoutPolicy` using the technique in the previous comment, ie make `onTimeoutAsync` extract the HttpRequestMessage from `context["HttpRequestMessageKey"]`.

---

@bramakrishna16 Hope that helps, and please let me know if you have any questions!
@bramakrishna16 How did you get on with this? Do you need any further information? Otherwise, I will close this in a few days' time.  Thanks

Just for posterity, the high cpu usage is likely a result of significant exception throwing happening based on @reisenberger 's thought on the `HttpClient.Timeout` being set to low.  Any app in .NET (Core or Framework) with an Exceptions/sec count of ~10 or higher has a significant and measurable impact on CPU.  This can be easily confirmed by looking in the Windows Performance Counters and looking at the "# of Exceps Thrown / sec" counter under the ".NET CLR Exceptions" counter category.  Just make sure to select your specific process to measure (the default setting is across all running processes).

Thanks @udlose . Or originally, it could equally have been the exceptions associated with https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/issues/26054

@CreepyGnome Adding examples to the unit testing page is a very good suggestion (we'll do).

Polly does already provide interfaces permitting the mockability you request.  I think the challenge is in discoverability (doco can help address).  

Policy configuration syntax does currently declare its return types as concrete classes ([example](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/7129e726d75086ab5eb270c798afc53b41f5dcbc/src/Polly/Retry/AsyncRetryTResultSyntax.cs#L1094)). But every such concrete policy class fulfils interfaces. Taking the same example: [here `IRetryPolicy<TResult>`](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/7129e726d75086ab5eb270c798afc53b41f5dcbc/src/Polly/Retry/AsyncRetryPolicy.cs#L59); and via here indirectly [`IAsyncPolicy<TResult>`](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/7129e726d75086ab5eb270c798afc53b41f5dcbc/src/Polly/AsyncPolicy.TResult.ExecuteOverloads.cs#L9). So:

```csharp
AsyncRetryPolicy<T> : IRetryPolicy<T>, IAsyncPolicy<T>
```

The step you likely need (we'll document) to get going with Polly and DI for testing, is to declare your polices as those [execution interfaces](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Polly-and-interfaces#the-execution-interfaces) where needed, eg instantiation:

```csharp
IAsyncPolicy<User> userRepoResiliencePolicy = GetRepoResiliencePolicy<User>();
```

storing:

```csharp
IAsyncPolicy<User> UserRepoResiliencePolicy { get; set; }
```

passing around by DI:

```csharp
public UserRepository(IAsyncPolicy<User> userRepoResiliencePolicy, ...) { ... }
```

Every other Polly policy type follows the same pattern. For example NoOpPolicy:

```csharp
AsyncNoOpPolicy<T> : INoOpPolicy<T>, IAsyncPolicy<T>
```

This is why you can swap `AsyncNoOpPolicy<T>` in for `AsyncRetryPolicy<T>`, if you manage your policies as instances of `IAsyncPolicy<T>`.

I've used `IAsyncPolicy<T>`, but the same principles apply with other execution interfaces (`ISyncPolicy`, `ISyncPolicy<T>`, `IAsyncPolicy`, `IAsyncPolicy<T>`), according to the policy you have configured.

For some immediate examples of that in unit tests, see [@bryanjhogan 's excellent blog post](https://nodogmablog.bryanhogan.net/2019/03/testing-your-code-when-using-polly/). This gives some concise examples of several styles of test, covering angles [1] [2] and [3] of the [wiki unit testing page](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Unit-testing-with-Polly) . 

I'm hoping this ^ is the magic ingredient you need to get going with Polly and DI for testing, but we will aim to add full examples, and others (DI with PolicyRegistry, and how to play that with testing, merits coverage too).

Thanks @CreepyGnome , the description just posted gives a great picture (no need to push on getting approvals for posting actual code if problematic - not unusual that companies have may have a view on that).

I'll post back with some concrete suggestions around the testing soon.

To whether Polly could adopt an instance/interface-based configuration approach, or introduce `IPolicyBuilder`:

One observation is that adopting `IPolicyBuilder` would mean that `IPolicyBuilder` would have to expose some properties which are currently `internal` - [`ExceptionPredicates`](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/5a5502b055248af43ca049ab1cabc91c4883da90/src/Polly/PolicyBuilder.cs#L20) and [`ResultPredicates`](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/5a5502b055248af43ca049ab1cabc91c4883da90/src/Polly/PolicyBuilder.cs#L105). 

Or alternatively keep them encapsulated but expose only methods that policies could use to evaluate exceptions/results against them, eg:

    bool IsExceptionHandled(Exception ex)

A problem is that this exposes methods on `IPolicyBuilder` that are not actually part of the user-experience we want of the builder syntax.  Users could be led down blind-alleys/dead-ends, as they try to construct the policy:

    Policy
        .Handle<FooException>()
        .ExceptionPredicates
        . // what do I do now?

or

    Policy
        .Handle<FooException>()
        .IsExceptionHandled(/* some exception instance */) // very confusing! - is this part of policy-building syntax or not?
        . // what do I do now?

This may not be insuperable, but is a concern.  An advantage of the current, 'closed' concrete builder classes is that there are no blind alleys in the syntax - users are inexorably guided to construct a finished policy.

([`EditorBrowsableAttribute`](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.componentmodel.editorbrowsableattribute) could be an angle on this - but it is not consistently honored.) 

(Explicit interface implementation to hide members could be another angle - but explicit interface implementation only works on classes/when the type in question is returned as a concrete class - and the goal of any change is specifically to work with an interface `IPolicyBuilder` instead.)

It's also possible that a .Net-core-style indented configuration syntax could avoid/minimise some of that problem:

    Policy.Handle(Action<IHandleConfiguration> configure)

leading to usage like:

    Policy.Handle(h => h.Handle<FooException>())

`IHandleConfiguration` is separate from `IPolicyBuilder`, so the blind-alleys do not arise.  This is the best candidate I have so far for such a transition, but it's less snappy, and is a major breaking change.

_EDIT:_ Moving fully to an instance/interface-based approach could read:

    new PolicyBuilder()
        .Handle<Fooexception>()
        // etc

(This would be a major breaking change.)

---

This is not a definitive statement on whether we go to `IPolicyBuilder`, just some initial observations. 

Definitely interested in community suggestions too - if there is some obvious better syntax we are missing?

Hi @CreepyGnome, Is there anything else we can follow up on, after the unit testing suggestions above?  



Good shout on improving the unit-testing documentation: that's been done, in [this page, with example code](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Unit-testing-with-Polly---with-examples).

Recasting the Policy `.Handle<>()` clauses to instance/inteface-based approaches: I've [lodged this in the roadmap](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Polly-Roadmap#consider-moving-handle-predicates-to-instanceinterface-configuration-style) with further commentary, as well as pointers back to here.

comments.body:
@slyce130 , good question.

Components of a `PolicyWrap` have no knowledge of the content of the other policies; only pointers to them. There is no in-built mechanism within `PolicyWrap` for a more-outer policy to know that a further-in policy might have matched its `Handle` clause.  So in this case, yes, if you want the `Handle` clauses of different policies to be mutually exclusive, you have to code them that way explicitly.

This flows from the fact that a PolicyWrap expresses nested execution (functional composition) rather than side-by-side switch/case or if-elseif-elseif-else logic. That was a design choice that brings lots of other benefits to PolicyWrap but (agreed) doesn't suit mutually-exclusive retry conditions well.

---

It could have been possible to introduce special rules about adjacent retry policies in a PolicyWrap (making them follow an if-elseif exclusivity), but that would have ended up mixing idioms - some cases of a PolicyWrap (or even parts of the same PolicyWrap) would have "nesting" meaning and others "parallel mutual exclusivity" meaning.  If we do more to support parallel-mutual-exclusivity in Polly, we might (thinking aloud) express it in a different way - perhaps as a new kind/variant of retry policy.  It happens not to be a particularly easy fit with the existing Polly syntax/architecture (keeping this response short, but can expand on that if anyone wants to explore).
Thanks for getting back to me. Looks like I'll be coding it explicitly.

No problem. It highlights the fact that Polly doesn't have a syntax story for the mutual-exclusive use case

If you had a lot of them (to code), it would probably be possible to write an extension method that converted the conditions (stated-without-explicit-exclusivity) into explicitly mutually exclusive steps in a PolicyWrap.

comments.body:
Polly TimeoutPolicy does not target this use case.

The simplest way to achieve this is to define your own timing-out CancellationToken and then use an existing form of retry policy with a handle clause along these lines:

    Policy
        .Handle<FooException>(e => !token.IsCancellationRequested)

Because CancellationTokens are single-use only, with an existing retry policy, you would need to define a new such policy instance per execution.

You could make a single policy instance which could be re-used, by defining your own custom policy for the behaviour: http://www.thepollyproject.org/2019/02/13/authoring-a-reactive-polly-policy-custom-policies-part-iii-2/

If you define a custom policy for this, we would love to include it in Polly-Contrib!: http://www.thepollyproject.org/2019/02/13/introducing-custom-polly-policies-and-polly-contrib-custom-policies-part-i/
Thanks, will look into doing that 😄

title: RetryUntilTimeout

comments.body:
@rojas8392 You have used an overload of `.WaitAndRetryAsync(...)` which takes a synchronous `onRetry:` delegate. That `onRetry:` delegate will only be called synchronously by the policy, so it will behave like an `async void` - it will return synchronously at the first `await` - not awaiting the call within it before the calling thread continues, as you observe.

Switch to using an overload of `.WaitAndRetryAsync(...)` where you specify an asynchronous, `onRetryAsync:`. For example [this overload](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/4db50346299f62c2373ceba99d2522a8171c9e27/src/Polly/Retry/AsyncRetrySyntax.cs#L381) (there are also many other variants if that is not exactly the one you need).
Thanks so much this fixed it!

comments.body:
Polly [contains no reference to System.Net.Http](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/eff944e005ba3e39c22f4f00e60b07baf57165ec/src/Polly/Polly.csproj). [Searching the Polly repo for http](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/search?q=http&unscoped_q=http) confirms there is no reference to `System.Net.Http`.

Polly [supports .Net Framework via .NET Standard targets](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/eff944e005ba3e39c22f4f00e60b07baf57165ec/src/Polly/Polly.csproj#L4).  My assumption is that the bridge from .NET Standard to .NET Framework for .NET4.6.1 is bringing in (that version of) `System.Net.Http` indirectly - _and/or_ that the MsBuild tooling is messing up the versions (as the issue you linked suggests). This is not something Polly can control; it is on the Microsoft side.

Are either of (1) and (2) below options for you?

(1) Add an explicit reference to `System.Net.Http`, the version you want to use, to your top-level project. (From the **Steps / Code to reproduce** which you quoted and the issue you linked, I suspect this may not be ~a complete~ any solution.)

(2) Upgrade to / support only .NET 4.7.2. This is a Microsoft recommendation (see [footnote 2 here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/net-standard#net-implementation-support)) for those on .NET4.6.1-4.7.1.  Because of the widely documented issues with .NET Framework 4.6.1-4.7.1 projects consuming .NET Std packages.

---

If those are not an option, a third option could be to explore whether this (3) would help:

(3) [Add explicit .NET Framework targets](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/issues/545) to Polly

If you wish to explore (3), please could you trial and report back whether this resolves your case or not. You can pull the Polly codebase from github to your local machine, add explicit framework targets as you require [here](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/eff944e005ba3e39c22f4f00e60b07baf57165ec/src/Polly/Polly.csproj#L4), run the build, and trial the nuget package which is generated in the `artifacts\nuget-package` folder. Start from the head of [this branch](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/commits/v711-or-v720), not `master`.

Based on reading https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/issues/25773, I cannot confidently say that (3) would solve the issue for you (the problem may still be caused by the interaction of MS Build/GAC and depend on the end-user's version of Visual Studio/MS Build). 

**_If_** (3) resolves your issue, it could be another reason for us to add .NET Framework targets to Polly.  We have been reluctant to do this, because it will force us to add a .NET Framework 4.7.2 target also (so that nuget does not downgrade those users to .NET4.6.1 dependencies); and that would change the .NET 4.7.2 experience to consuming framework instead of .NET Standard 2.0. That is a (theoretically) unnecessary change for .NET 4.7.2 users, but the nuget tooling would force us to do it.

I haven't been working in .NET Framework for some months now, so all community feedback is welcome.

I tried variations of 1) but didn't work. I think the best approach we should take is 2) as is recommended by MS and .net is moving forward.

Having said that, I'll give it a shot to 3) and will let you know my findings.

All right, so I've tried adding the 461 target (branch [here](https://github.com/afcruzs/Polly/commit/186e2f589459bd72fffc29c6bfa48d88e037fca7)). Indeed the manifest looks like what I'm expecting on the minimal repro library after using the nuget built locally:

```
.assembly extern System.Net.Http
{
  .publickeytoken = (B0 3F 5F 7F 11 D5 0A 3A )                         // .?_....:
  .ver 4:1:1:2
}
```
Thanks!  Good to know.  Ok, I will consult with the other Polly team key stakeholder whether we are good to add .NET Framework targets back in, seems like it would help here.

@afcruzs We experienced the same. @jglinsek tracked down a way to resolve it in the short-term by adding an explicit binding redirect to downgrade system.net.http to 4.0.0.0

```
      <dependentAssembly>
        <assemblyIdentity name="System.Net.Http" publicKeyToken="b03f5f7f11d50a3a" culture="neutral" />
        <bindingRedirect oldVersion="0.0.0.0-4.2.0.0" newVersion="4.0.0.0" />
      </dependentAssembly>
```

This may not work for your use case but, if so, it might be a way forward in the short-term. This issue affects us on 461 and 472.
Polly v7.2.0 [has been published](https://www.nuget.org/packages/polly) with .NET Framework targets 4.6.1 and 4.7.2 now supported natively as part of the nuget package.  Should resolve this issue.

comments.body:
Hi @andreybutko  Is this the kind of pattern you are looking for?

    private Task<T> Validate<T>(Func<Task<T>> func) => Policy.WrapAsync(retryPolicy, breakPolicy, authorisationEnsuringPolicy).ExecuteAsync(func);

An appropriate way to handle this is to put the re-authorisation policy nearest executing the underlying delegate (as above code does) - because you don't want a simple (successful) not-authorised-then-reauthorise cycle to count as a failure against the circuit-breaker.  It also means you can define one retry for re-authorisation, but multiple retries for other failures - as your existing, separate `retryPolicy` does.  You can [use the same kind of policy more than once in a PolicyWrap](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/PolicyWrap#using-the-same-type-of-policy-more-than-once-in-a-wrap), as my example above shows with retry policies.  

If you want to expand your existing `retryPolicy` and `breakPolicy` to handle result codes as well as exceptions, see the documentation [here](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly#step-1b-optionally-specify-return-results-you-want-to-handle).  There is a code example titled `// Handle both exceptions and return values in one policy`. Define a policy handling both exceptions and results something like this:

    var policyToHandleBothExceptionsAndResults = Policy
        .Handle<HttpRequestException>()
        .OrResult<HttpResponseMessage>(r => httpStatusCodesWorthRetrying.Contains(r.StatusCode))
        .RetryAsync(...);

---

Here are links to three blogs which provide fully worked examples:

+ https://nodogmablog.bryanhogan.net/2017/05/re-authorization-and-onretry-with-polly/
+ https://diaryofadev.net/2017/05/oath-with-polly/
+ https://www.jerriepelser.com/blog/refresh-google-access-token-with-polly/

Hi @jaumemilian . Polly does not provide a specific API for evicting cache entries. So far, it takes the view that, when you created the cache Policy, you had access to the underlying cache (`IMemoryCache` or `IDistributedCache`), and you can use this directly to invalidate specific cache entries.

---

We could happily add `Remove(string)` and `Remove(string, CancellationToken)` overloads to the [`ISyncCacheProvider`](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/eff944e005ba3e39c22f4f00e60b07baf57165ec/src/Polly/Caching/ISyncCacheProvider.cs) and [`IAsyncCacheProvider`](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/eff944e005ba3e39c22f4f00e60b07baf57165ec/src/Polly/Caching/IAsyncCacheProvider.cs) interfaces respectively.  

Then, `CachePolicy` (and its variants) could also have methods `Remove(string)` and `RemoveAsync(string, CancellationToken)` which could chain on to those.

We would also have to update the two cache providers from the App-vNext team, to match those changes: [Polly.Caching.MemoryCache](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly.Caching.MemoryCache) and [Polly.Caching.IDistributedCache](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly.Caching.IDistributedCache).

Marking this **up-for-grabs**, as it's a great first issue for anyone to take on!  (I am focusing on pushing out Distributed Circuit Breaker at the moment.)

Hi,
I would like to work on this issue. Can you please give me some more insights on how I should proceed with it ?
@komalg1 Thanks! I'll aim to add some more notes in the next couple of days/as soon as I can get time.

Thanks again @komalg1 for offering to contribute!

First, see our general notes on [Git workflow](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Git-Workflow) and [configuring line endings](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Fix-your-line-endings%21).

If this is your first open source contribution, google can return lots of general guidance on beginning contributing to OSS - but do fire away with any specific questions.

I'm not sure how familiar you are with Polly, so if any of the below is too obvious, bear with me. 

The below looks to me like a route through what's needed, but if something isn't making sense, feel free to ask more questions; or if it doesn't look like a good first issue, again, feel free to say.

### Start

+ Understand [the respective roles of CachePolicy and its CacheProviders](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Cache). CachePolicy contains the cache-aside logic - try to get the result from cache; if result was retrieved from underlying system instead, store it in the cache. CacheProviders are different actual cache implementations (memory cache; distributed cache etc), and not stored in this repo.
+ Find `ISyncCacheProvider` and `IAsyncCacheProvider` [in the codebase](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/tree/master/src/Polly/Caching)
+ In your branch (see Gitflow above!), add `void Remove(string)` overloads to the `ISyncCacheProvider` and `ISyncCacheProvider<TResult>` interfaces; and `Task RemoveAsync(string, CancellationToken)` to the similar `IAsyncCacheProvider` interfaces.

At this point the `Polly` project (but not `Polly.Specs`) should compile.

### Make cache policy classes have Remove methods chaining on to cache provider Remove methods

+ Create `IAsyncCachePolicy` and `IAsyncCachePolicy<TResult>` interfaces (they're missing; follow the pattern for `ISyncCachePolicy` and `ISyncCachePolicy<TResult>`), and make `AsyncCachePolicy : IAsyncCachePolicy` and `AsyncCachePolicy<TResult> : IAsyncCachePolicy<TResult>`.
+ Add a `void Remove(string)` overload to `ICachePolicy`. 
+ Add a `Task Remove(string, CancellationToken)` overload to `IAsyncCachePolicy`. 
+ Fulfil those methods in `CachePolicy`, `CachePolicy<TResult>`, `AsyncCachePolicy` and `AsyncCachePolicy<TResult>` just by delegating to the relevant overloads on the cache provider which the policies store.

Again, at this point the `Polly` project (but not `Polly.Specs`) should compile.

### Unit tests

+ Because the only action in CachePolicy implementations will be to delegate any `Remove(...)` or `RemoveAsync(...)` calls to the configured cache provider, it would be acceptable, for tests, to use Moq just to verify that the call is delegated in that way.
+ Implementations of the remove methods in `StubCacheProvider` will be needed for completeness. (_This is an intentionally naive non-concurrency-safe in-memory cache provider implementation, which serves as something simple for tests_ while avoiding getting into the differences between MemoryCache in .Net Framework and .Net Core. For Remove: obvious, simple implementations will do.)
+ Implementations of the remove methods in `StubErroringCacheProvider` will be needed for completeness. They can just delegate to the wrapped `StubCacheProvider`. I guess I'm proposing that cache policies won't do any special handling of errors thrown by Remove calls - they'll just let any errors bubble outwards.  (The policies do special handling of errors during _get_ or _put_, because we elected that cache errors should not bring down the whole call through Polly.)

Hi,

First of all, thanks for your offer to develop that.

Let me try to clarify what was my first request looking for:

In the IDistributedCache, there is already a mechanism to remove cache entries if you know the key of the entry you want to remove.

`_cacheInstance.Remove(key)`

What I was looking for in my question was a nice feature that is available for the IMemoryCache, where you can associate several cache entries to one "CancellationTokenSource", and just cancelling that CancellationTokenSource, all the cache entries associated are automatically removed from the cache [https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.caching.memory.memorycacheentryextensions.addexpirationtoken?view=aspnetcore-2.2](url)

We can't find that feature in the IDistriburedCache, and I just was wondering if could be Polly was offering on top of IDistributedCache something similar to that

Thanks for +1 :eyes: spotting what I missed!  Those interfaces are not yet there; they would need adding.  Looking at the patterns again, we would need:

    ISyncCachePolicy : ICachePolicy
    ISyncCachePolicy<TResult> : ISyncCachePolicy
    IAsyncCachePolicy : ICachePolicy

Thus: `ICachePolicy` is just a marker interface for "this is a cache policy" (it might in future contain something that is common to cache policies whether sync or async).  Then, the new `Remove(string)` overload goes on `ISyncCachePolicy` (not `ICachePolicy` as I originally said).

    // outside loop
    var policy = Policy
